title: The Father Knows More About This
author: Moore, Brandon
summary: Writing to fellow men, Brandon Moore describes a personal season of discarding decades-old possessions he came to see as obstacles to Christlikeness, framing the discipline of fatherhood and marriage as placing others' needs above one's own. He connects the practice to 1 Corinthians' call to put away 'childish things' and to act like men 'in love,' and describes the unexpected ripple effect on his wife and son, more conversations, not necessarily instant resolution. He closes with a direct challenge to male readers to ask their wives what 'childish things' they still cling to and to sit with the answer rather than defend against it.
points: Frames good brotherhood, marriage, and fatherhood as the discipline of placing others' needs above one's own.
Describes a personal purge of long-held possessions as an act of sacrifice tied to spiritual growth, not mere decluttering.
Uses 1 Corinthians 13 and 16 to link 'acting like men' explicitly to love, not stoicism or toughness.
Ends with a direct challenge: ask your wife what childish things you still hold onto, and actually listen without defending yourself.
quotes: Indeed, to be a good father a man absolutely must learn to place the needs of his children higher than his own.
It is called sacrificing myself, so that I may become more like Christ.

The leadership of a man is a bizarre thing when it is being performed as nearly correct as a man can perform. They know, having witnessed a genuine difficulty for me, that faithfulness to Christ is all important, even when it requires sacrifice.

Be on the alert, stand firm in the faith, act like men, be strong. All that you do must be done in love." (1 Corinthians 16:13-14). Whatever that means to you, according to the doctrine which has fostered immense growth in those that follow it, it requires that it be done in love.
Tonight, if you dare, ask your wife what childish things you employ. Ask for clarification on what things you enjoy that, from her perspective, are those of a boy and not a man.
